introduction-the-push-and-pray-loop.core: YAML pipelines can only be tested by pushing them to the CI server. Dagger turns pipelines into real code (Go, Python, TypeScript) that runs in containers identically on a laptop and in any CI.

first_principles.problem: Debugging a pipeline means commit 'fix ci', push, wait 10 minutes, repeat.
derivation: Execute every step **in containers** through the Dagger engine.
Call it from **any CI** with one command.

analogy.title: Rehearsing at home vs. only on stage
analogy.story: With Dagger you rehearse the whole show at home, exactly as it will run on stage.
analogy.breaks: It's another tool to learn, and teams need SDK language familiarity.

example.title: Fixing a pipeline bug
flow: After: `dagger call test` locally, fixed in 5 minutes

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Pipeline development gets an inner loop.

check.q: What core problem does Dagger address?
check.a: Pipelines that can only be tested by pushing YAML to CI.

architecture-the-engine-and-the-sdks.core: Dagger is client/server: SDKs in your language build a graph of container operations through a GraphQL API, and the Dagger Engine (BuildKit-based) executes that DAG in containers, with caching and parallelism.

first_principles.problem: You need to know where code runs and why the results are identical everywhere.
truths: An API decouples languages from the engine.
derivation: Calls are **lazy**; nothing runs until the result is needed.

analogy.title: An architect and a construction crew
analogy.story: The architect (SDK) draws plans in any language; the crew (engine) builds them the same way on every site.
analogy.breaks: The engine needs a container runtime (Docker or similar) wherever it runs.

example.title: A Python Dagger function

steps.label: Run
steps.detail: `dagger call test --src=.` locally or in CI.

example.outcome: you understand why Dagger is portable and fast.

check.a: The Dagger Engine, built on BuildKit, running operations in containers.

ci-as-code-programmable-pipelines.core: Real code gives pipelines loops, conditionals, functions, types, tests and packages, so dynamic logic (build only changed services in a monorepo) is natural instead of YAML templating spaghetti.

first_principles.problem: Expressing 'for each changed service, build and test it' in YAML needs generated YAML or brittle matrix hacks.
truths: Programming languages are made for logic.
Code can be unit-tested and reused.

analogy.title: A spreadsheet macro vs. copy-pasted formulas
analogy.story: One function handles every row, instead of a formula pasted into each cell.
analogy.breaks: Too much cleverness makes pipelines hard to read, so keep them simple.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Parallel tests for just the changed services, with no YAML generation.

check.q: Why is dynamic monorepo logic easier in Dagger than in YAML?
check.a: Real code has loops, conditionals and functions, which YAML lacks.

caching-speed-by-default.core: Every Dagger operation is content-addressed: if its inputs haven't changed, the cached result is reused. Cache volumes persist dependency directories, so fast pipelines are the default rather than hand-tuned.

first_principles.problem: Hand-maintained cache keys in YAML are error-prone and often miss.
truths: Package managers benefit from persistent directories.
derivation: **Layer cache**: identical operations are skipped automatically.
**Cache volumes** (withMountedCache) for node_modules, ~/.cache/pip, the Go mod cache.
**Order operations** so stable steps come first.
Persist the engine's cache across CI runs.

analogy.title: A chef's mise en place
analogy.story: Ingredients prepped yesterday and unchanged today are reused rather than chopped again.
analogy.breaks: Ephemeral CI runners lose the cache unless the engine state is persisted or Dagger Cloud is used.

example.title: Caching pip downloads

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Installs are near-instant when requirements haven't changed.

example.outcome: fast pipelines without manual cache keys.

check.q: Why copy requirements.txt before the full source in Dagger or Docker?
check.a: So the dependency install step stays cached when only application code changes.

integrating-dagger-into-existing-ci-syst.core: Dagger isn't a CI replacement. Your existing CI (GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins) still handles triggers, secrets and runners, and simply calls `dagger call ...`. Pipeline logic becomes portable across all of them.

first_principles.problem: Migrating CI vendors means rewriting every pipeline in new YAML.
truths: CI systems are good at events and scheduling.
A single entry point simplifies migration.
derivation: CI YAML is **thin**: checkout plus `dagger call`.
Migrating vendors means changing **only the thin wrapper**.

analogy.title: A universal power adapter
analogy.story: The device (pipeline) stays the same; only the plug changes for each country (CI vendor).
analogy.breaks: CI-native features (matrix UI, annotations) need some glue code.

example.title: GitHub Actions calling Dagger

steps.label: Migrate
steps.detail: GitLab gets the same `dagger call test --src=.` in its own YAML.

code.text:
jobs:
  ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dagger/dagger-for-github@v6
        with:
          verb: call
          args: test --src=.
        env: { DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN: "${{ secrets.DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN }}" }

example.outcome: pipelines are portable across CI systems.

check.q: What stays in your CI system's YAML when using Dagger?
check.a: Triggers, secrets, runner selection, and a single `dagger call` invocation.
